records.name_note: The dedicated pages lead with snow-in-summer. NC State's Description opens "Snow-in-summer is a low-growing, herbaceous perennial" and explains the name ("the numerous blooms on Snow-in-summer form a carpet of white, hence its common name"); its page-title parenthetical and Common Name(s) list are alphabetized, so Dusty Miller comes first there. RHS's page renders snow-in-summer beneath its Cerastium tomentosum heading (browser title 'Cerastium tomentosum | snow-in-summer') and lists dusty miller under Other common names. Missouri Botanical Garden's Noteworthy Characteristics prose reads 'Cerastium tomentosum, known as snow-in-summer'. Dusty Miller is therefore not used as the primary name here. The name is title-cased as Snow-in-Summer, as this catalog lands Love-in-a-Mist.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: no admissible source checked (NC State, MoBot, RHS) carries a Poison block or any cat/dog toxicity statement for Cerastium tomentosum; left null. No Jacobaea (dusty miller) toxicity is carried over.
is_edible: no source addresses eating this plant; left null.

is_houseplant is false: no source frames it as a houseplant; NC State's Plant Type field (Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial) and USDA zones 3a-7b describe an in-ground ground cover/rock-garden perennial.

Spread habit as sources word it: NC State says it 'can be weedy in locations with cooler summer climates where the plant is robust' and tags it spreading, weedy and mat forming, and says it spreads by underground runners; MoBot says it spreads by runners and 'is not considered to be invasive in hot climates where it is less robust than in cooler northern climates'. Both say less invasive, more compact cultivars exist (cultivars are not the species).

Size disagreement: NC State gives height 0.5-1 ft and width 0.75-1.5 ft (6-12 in, 9-18 in, used here); MoBot gives height 0.5-1.0 ft and spread 0.75-1.0 ft; RHS gives Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres and Max Spread 1-1.5 metres (about 3.9-19.7 in and 39.4-59.1 in), a notably wider spread, likely UK-grown. The NC State dimensions are used as the anchor.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists both Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours), but MoBot (Sun: Full sun) and RHS (Position Full sun) list full sun only, so part_shade is left out. NC State also says it does not perform well in a location with insufficient sunlight.
soil_ph_min/max: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and RHS lists pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral; open-ended bands give no usable bounds. Left null.

water_regime and watering intervals: MoBot's structured Water field reads Dry, but this is a site-condition rating for an in-ground plant, not a watering instruction; no source gives a watering regime or interval. Left null.

humidity_need: NC State says the plant does not perform well in climates with high humidity (tagged humidity intolerant), and MoBot says it performs poorly in hot, humid summers; this is outdoor climate guidance, not an indoor humidity percentage or need. Left null.

chill_damage_f: MoBot gives winter hardiness to USDA Zone 2 and NC State zones 3a-7b; these are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures. Left null. Day/night temperature ranges, light in foot-candles, direct sun hours maximum, fertilizing: no admissible source figures; left null.

Kept separate from weedy mouse-ear chickweeds (Cerastium fontanum and others): NC State lists Wooly Mouse-Ear Chickweed as a common name of this exact species, but no cross-species contrast was sourced.

This is the catalog's first Cerastium; no cross-check against other Cerastium entries was needed. A MoBot page and an NC State page exist for this exact taxon; the RHS page used is the Cerastium tomentosum page (not var. columnae). Clemson, PSU, UMD, UF/IFAS and UGA were not found to carry a dedicated page for this taxon (PSU only lists it in a heat-and-drought plant list, not used).

The auditor offered an optional MoBot soil_drainage citation ('Best grown in dry, sandy, well-drained soils in full sun.'); Missouri Botanical Garden refuses this machine, so it was not added. That MoBot sentence is already in the record as the researcher's outdoor_sun_exposure citation, and the auditor reports reading it live.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated Dianthus plumarius page lists Cottage Pink first in its alphabetized Common Name(s) list (Cottage Pink, Feathered Pink, Garden Pink, Grass Pink, Pheasant's Eye Pink, Pinks, Scotch Pink, Wild Pink), and its browser title repeats that list in parentheses. The same page also lists 'Cottage Pink' as a cultivar under Cultivars / Varieties. RHS's dedicated page shows clove pink as the common name under its Dianthus plumarius heading (browser title "Dianthus plumarius | clove pink") and lists cottage pink first among its Other common names. Cottage Pink is used here because it leads NC State's list. No Missouri Botanical Garden species page could be read, so MoBot's lead name is not reflected. Distinct from Dianthus caryophyllus (Carnation), Dianthus chinensis (Chinese Pink), Dianthus gratianopolitanus (Cheddar Pink), Dianthus deltoides (Maiden Pink) and Dianthus barbatus (Sweet William), already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu, dedicated Dianthus plumarius page), under the "Poisonous to Humans" heading, so the severity rating is human-scoped: "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: "It causes low toxicity only if eaten. Skin irritation is minor or lasting only for a few minutes, vomiting." Poison Toxic Principle: Triterpenoid saponins. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Leaves. The Plant Type field lists Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. Separately from the human block, the page's Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses (also shown as the tags #problem for dogs, #problem for horses, #problem for cats); it gives no animal-specific symptom list or severity, so cat/dog severity is unknown. RHS (rhs.org.uk dedicated page) lists under Potentially harmful: "Humans/Pets: Skin allergen; wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and refers readers to the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for pets. Its Pets scope names no cat or dog, so it does not by itself support cat/dog toxicity. Edibility note: NC State says petals can be made into cordials, syrups, sauces and vinegars while the leaves are the poisonous part.
unknowns: No Missouri Botanical Garden page for the species itself could be read: plantfinder.mobot.org refused connection from this environment and the only MoBot pages found by search were cultivar pages ('Itsaul White', 'Pheasant's Eye'), which are not admissible for species facts. No Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA dedicated Dianthus plumarius page turned up (only genus or multi-species pages), so NC State and RHS are the only sources used.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source addresses indoor culture, and NC State's Plant Type field (Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous) and USDA zones 3a-9b describe an outdoor ground cover.

toxic_to_pets is true on NC State's Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs entries (Problems field and tags) for this exact species; those entries carry no symptoms or severity. The Low severity, symptoms (low toxicity only if eaten, minor skin irritation, vomiting), triterpenoid saponins, contact dermatitis and leaves-as-poison-part all come from the Poisonous to Humans block. RHS's skin-allergen handling warning is scoped Humans/Pets and names no cat or dog, so it does not by itself support toxic_to_pets.

is_edible is true only for petals (NC State Uses (Ethnobotany): cordials, syrups, sauces, vinegars); NC State lists leaves as the poisonous part and the plant is tagged Poisonous. Do not present the whole plant as edible.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. RHS's dedicated Lomelosia caucasica page renders "garden scabious" as the subtitle beneath its H1 and lists "Caucasian scabious, white bonnets" under Other common names. NC State's dedicated page renders a Common Name(s) list (Perennial Scabious, Pincushion Flower, White Bonnets), alphabetized and in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, so its first entry is Perennial Scabious; "Pincushion Flower" is second there and does not appear as a name on the RHS page. Both pages treat Lomelosia caucasica as the accepted name: NC State shows Scabiosa caucasica as "Previously known as", RHS lists Scabiosa caucasica under Synonyms, and the RHS profile for Lomelosia caucasica carries Name Status Correct.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden (plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be read: curl failed TLS verification (exit 60, unable to verify the first certificate) and WebFetch failed the same way, so no MoBot content is used and MoBot's common-name lead is unconfirmed. Its page found by search is titled Scabiosa caucasica (the former name), not Lomelosia caucasica.

No dedicated Lomelosia caucasica or Scabiosa caucasica page was found on Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD or UGA. A search returned only the UF/IFAS page for the different species Scabiosa atropurpurea, which was not used.

toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible are null because no admissible source for this exact taxon addresses toxicity or eating. NC State's page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags.
is_houseplant is false: no admissible source frames the plant as a houseplant. NC State (Plant Type Herbaceous Perennial, USDA zones 3a-8b) and RHS treat it as an in-ground herbaceous perennial.

Heat and humidity: NC State's description says "It also is intolerant of high heat and humidity." and "The plant dies out in warm, coastal plains gardens and should be protected from wet, winter weather." These are tolerance statements, not a need or a damage-onset temperature, so humidity_need, humidity_pct_*, day/night temps and chill_damage_f are left null. NC State's page title parenthetical is the only place its common names are comma-joined, and the list is alphabetized.

water_regime and all watering fields are null. NC State and RHS give no watering instruction. NC State says only "Good drainage is especially important because the plant will rot in wet soil." (a soil-drainage statement), and RHS gives Moisture: Well-drained.

soil_drainage fast is an inference from NC State's description (light, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; rots in wet soil) plus its Drought tag under Resistance To Challenges. NC State's structured field is only Good Drainage, with no Moisture field. RHS says Moisture Well-drained. If a stricter reading is wanted, treat this as bare well-drained (null).

Size: NC State's Dimensions block (Height and Width both 1 ft. 6 in. - 2 ft. 0 in., so 18-24 in.) is used. RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in), which is wider and not used. NC State's prose says 'a mature height of 2 feet with an equal width'.

soil_ph_max is null: NC State lists Alkaline (>8.0), which is open-ended, and RHS lists pH Alkaline or Neutral. soil_ph_min 6.0 comes from the closed lower bound of NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band. No Acid band is listed.

outdoor_sun_exposure keeps full_sun and part_shade from NC State's structured Light field (Full sun; Partial Shade). The audit asked to drop part_shade because RHS's structured Position field lists only Full sun (Aspect South–facing or West–facing) and NC State's tags frame shade as a tolerance ("#partial shade tolerant"). part_shade was kept: NC State's tag row frames full sun the same way ("#full sun tolerant"), the only structured field excluding part_shade is RHS's, a UK rating, no second North American structured field could be read (MoBot refuses this machine), and no page carries a scorch or flop warning against shade; NC State's "intolerant of high heat and humidity" is a climate caution. This follows Carnation (b96). The hour ranges inside NC State's light labels are the site-wide legend, so direct_sun_hours_max is left null.

Fertilizing, light in foot-candles, cool-rest and winter-protection temperatures are not stated numerically by any readable admissible source, so those fields are null. NC State's winter mulch advice and RHS's "Protect from winter wet" are not a damage-onset temperature.

records.name_note: NC State's page-title parenthetical and its rendered Common Name(s) list both give seven names in alphabetical order, starting with Blue Lungwort; NC State's Description opens with Lungwort, which is used here as common_name. RHS's dedicated page leads with common lungwort (title 'Pulmonaria officinalis | common lungwort'), so the two dedicated sources differ on the lead name. Distinct from Mertensia virginica (Virginia Bluebells), already in this catalog, whose NC State name list includes Smooth Lungwort.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Edibility field reads: "The leaves are edible." Its Description repeats the statement: "Its leaves are edible. Although quite bland, they are low in fiber and can be added to other ingredients in salads." and its tags include #edible leaves. The statement names the leaves only; NC State says nothing about eating any other part, and states no preparation condition (cooking, quantity). The same Description records a medicinal-use history, not a recommendation: "Its common name, Lungwort, is derived from Medieval herbalists who believed that the plant was effective in the treatment of lung diseases." The page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags, so no toxicity severity, symptom list or poison-part list exists on it. RHS's dedicated page carries no edibility statement and no Potentially harmful entry.
unknowns: RHS's dedicated page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/14153/pulmonaria-officinalis/details) was read at landing: it corroborates NC State on sun (Position Full shade, Partial shade), drainage (Moisture Moist but well–drained) and size (Max Height and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres), rates the plant H6, and disagrees with NC State on acid soil (pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral). The researcher had tried only guessed RHS slugs without the numeric id. MoBot / plantfinder.mobot.org (connection error), Clemson HGIC (403), UMD (404) and UF/IFAS pages could not be loaded by the researcher or are not species pages.

Jerusalem Sage and Jerusalem Cowslip appear in both NC State's and RHS's name lists for this species. No admissible source page for Phlomis fruticosa or Primula was read, so no cross-species point is asserted in name_note.

toxic_to_pets is null: neither the NC State page nor the RHS page has a Poison block, a Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag or a Potentially harmful entry. is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field (Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial) and USDA zones 3a-8b describe an outdoor perennial; its Container and Patio Landscape Location values are outdoor uses, and no source mentions indoor growing.

Edibility: NC State says the leaves are edible, with no preparation conditions and nothing about other parts; RHS's dedicated page says nothing about eating the plant. NC State's medicinal-history sentence (Medieval herbalists' belief about lung diseases) is carried in toxicity_detail as history only.
soil_base is null: NC State gives Soil Texture High Organic Matter but no potting or bed medium statement, and Container, Patio and Woodland are all listed Landscape Locations.

soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's Good Drainage + Moist pair. Moist is not stated as a cultivation requirement, so moisture_retentive is not used. The Description warns soils that are too wet or too dry are detrimental, and that root rot may occur when soil remains wet.

water_regime is null: the page gives no watering instruction, only soil adjectives and the tags dry soils intolerant and wet soils intolerant. Day-interval and dry-down fields are null because this is an in-ground perennial and no source frames watering that way.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists only Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), implying no acid soil, while RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'; the sources disagree on the floor and NC State's Alkaline band is open-ended.

Temperature, humidity, indoor light, fertilizer and chill-damage fields are null: no admissible source stated them. The USDA zones 3a-8b on NC State are a hardiness range, not a damage onset.

Size comes from NC State's Dimensions block, 0 ft 6 in to 1 ft 0 in tall (6-12 in) and 1 ft 0 in to 1 ft 6 in wide (12-18 in). The Trevi Fountain cultivar is listed on the page but no cultivar sizes were used.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's page-title parenthetical for Salvia leucantha lists "Mexican Bush Sage, Velvet Sage" (the Common Name(s) list there is alphabetized). RHS's page title for the exact taxon is "Salvia leucantha | Mexican bush sage". UF/IFAS's dedicated page (FP527) leads its Common name(s) list with "Mexican sage" and lists "Mexican bush sage" third. Two of the three reachable pages therefore lead with Mexican bush sage, which is the name used here. Missouri Botanical Garden's page could not be loaded.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid=281422) could not be loaded: the sandbox fetch failed on a TLS certificate error, so no MoBot claim or quote is used. Clemson HGIC has no dedicated page for this species that loaded (the factsheet URL returned 403); only a genus page appeared in search, which is not admissible.

Hardiness has no schema field; as stated by sources: NC State says "It is only hardy from the lower Piedmont to the coastal plain, and extreme winters may kill it." and lists USDA zones 7b-10b; UF/IFAS lists zones 7 through 11 and says the plant is killed to the ground by freezing temperatures in the northern part of its range; NC State tags it #tender perennial and #annual (NC State Life Cycle lists Annual and Perennial). RHS carries an H2 rating (UK conditions). None of these is a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null.

Toxicity: no admissible source reachable states toxicity or non-toxicity for Salvia leucantha (NC State page has no Poison or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs fields). toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null.
Edibility: no source reachable addresses eating this plant; is_edible is null.

Size conflict: mature_height_in/mature_spread_in use NC State prose "2 to 3 feet tall and wide" (24-36 in; the page has no structured Dimensions block). RHS gives Max Height 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in) and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in); UF/IFAS gives Height 1 to 2 feet and Spread 2 to 3 feet. Sources disagree.

Watering: NC State prose "rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil" is a soil preference and UF/IFAS says "regular watering" with drought tolerance; no source gives a watering regime that maps cleanly, so water_regime and all watering/fertilizer fields are null. RHS Moisture reads "Moist but well-drained".

Soil pH: NC State lists Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), so it gives an open-ended ceiling and a 6.0 floor; RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, which contradicts that floor. With no usable ceiling and a disputed floor, both pH fields are null.

Sun: NC State and RHS list full sun and partial shade; UF/IFAS lists full sun only. NC State's Partial Shade category (2-6 hours direct sun) is mapped to part_shade. NC State prose adds that it 'tolerates afternoon shade in regions with high summer heat' (conditional, not used for extra values). direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures are in NC State's generic light-category legend.

RHS Cultivation paragraph is genus-level tender-salvia boilerplate and was not used. is_houseplant is false: no source frames it as a houseplant, and NC State's Plant Type field (Annual, Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Shrub) and USDA zones 7b-10b describe an outdoor border plant. Temperature, humidity and light-fc fields have no species-specific admissible support and are null.
I did not find an admissible source page contrasting this species with Salvia mexicana, so no confusion claim is made.

records.name_note: Sources differ on the lead name. RHS's dedicated Echinops ritro page leads with the subtitle "small globe thistle", and MoBot's dedicated page carries a single Common Name line reading "small globe thistle". NC State's page-title parenthetical and its Common Name(s) list are alphabetized (Blue Hedgehog, Globe Flower, Globe Thistle, Small Globe Thistle, Steel Globe Thistle). common_name follows RHS and MoBot. NC State's Description calls the species "Globe thistle", and NC State and RHS list "Globe Flower" as an alternate name for this species.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Echinops ritro page carries the tags "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses" and "#non-toxic for dogs" in its Tags block. The same Tags block also lists #pollinator plant, #herbaceous perennial, #rabbit resistant and #deer resistant. NC State has no Poison block for this species. No admissible source states a poison part, symptom list or severity rating. No source gives a handling warning for the spiny leaves; NC State describes "stiff, spiny leaves" and MoBot "Coarse, spiny, deeply-dissected, gray-green leaves". The non-toxic claim comes only from NC State's tags; RHS and MoBot say nothing on toxicity.
unknowns: No source states edibility, so is_edible is null.

is_houseplant is false: no source frames it as a houseplant; NC State's Plant Type (Perennial), USDA zones 3a-8b and Landscape Theme (Cottage Garden, Cutting Garden, Pollinator Garden) describe an in-ground perennial.

toxic_to_pets=false rests only on NC State's cat and dog tags; RHS and MoBot are silent on toxicity. There is no handling note about the spiny leaves beyond the descriptions, and no poison parts or symptoms are stated.

outdoor_sun_exposure is limited to full_sun. RHS's structured Position lists Full sun and Partial shade, but NC State's structured Light field and MoBot's Sun field list full sun only. NC State's prose and tag say partial shade is tolerated, which is a tolerance aside and was left out.

Size sources disagree. NC State gives a height of 3 to 4 ft (36-48 in) and a width of 2 to 2.5 ft (24-30 in), which MoBot's 3.00 to 4.00 ft height and 2.00 to 2.50 ft spread match. RHS gives a Max Height of 0.5-1 m (19.7-39.4 in) and a Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 m (3.9-19.7 in). The NC State figures were used.
soil_ph is null. NC State's only pH value is the open-ended band Acid (<6.0), and RHS lists pH as Acid or Alkaline or Neutral.

soil_drainage=fast is a judgement call. NC State tags Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry and warns against wet, soggy soil, and MoBot says well-drained. No source describes wet tolerance. The prose phrase 'medium-moist to dry' could also support moderate.

water_regime=dry_surface_between reads MoBot's structured Water field 'Dry to medium'. No source gives a watering instruction, and drought tolerance was not used as evidence. It could instead be read as mid-scale.
Hardiness ratings and zones (NC State zones 3a-8b, MoBot zone 3 to 8, RHS H7) are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures, so chill_damage_f is null.
No temperature, humidity, indoor light, fertilizer or watering-interval data exist in the admissible pages, so those fields are null.
Cultivars 'Veitch's Blue' and 'Platinum Blue' appear on the pages, and RHS lists 'Veitch's Blue' misapplied under this species. No cultivar data were used.
Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA pages for Echinops ritro were not located. Only NC State, RHS and MoBot dedicated pages were used.

plantfinder.mobot.org could not be fetched with certificate verification from this environment; it was read with verification skipped, and the MoBot quotes could not be run through the project's mechanical verify_quotes check. MoBot's Common Names popup text was not quoted.

NC State's Common Name(s) list and RHS's Other common names field include 'globe flower' as an alternate name; it was not used as the primary name because RHS and MoBot lead with 'small globe thistle'.
